title: The fairest rules are the ones you’d pick before knowing who you are
body: In his 1971 book A Theory of Justice, John Rawls proposed a thought experiment: choose the basic rules of society from behind a ‘veil of ignorance’, without knowing your gender, ethnicity, talents, wealth or even your idea of a good life. Since nobody can rig the rules in their own favor, Rawls argued, whatever people would agree to there counts as fair.

slides.heading: Rawls’s answer
slides.text: He argued people would choose equal basic liberties for all, and accept inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged: the ‘difference principle’.

slides.heading: Same veil, other answer
slides.text: Economist John Harsanyi had used a similar device earlier and concluded that rational people would maximize average well-being, a utilitarian result.

slides.heading: The hidden variable
slides.text: The split comes down to risk: Rawls assumed people would guard against the worst outcome, while Harsanyi assumed they would weigh the odds.

slides.heading: Older roots
slides.text: Similar ideas of impartial judgment appear in Kant and in Adam Smith’s ‘impartial spectator’, though Rawls coined the phrase ‘veil of ignorance’.

slides.question: Why did Rawls and Harsanyi reach different answers from the same veil?
slides.explanation: Rawls assumed people would guard against the worst outcome; Harsanyi assumed they would weigh the odds and maximize average well-being.
